the csv module does the reading and the writing
cases.describe: the csv module, with the files opened in a with block

practice1.hint: A CSV file's first line is usually names for the columns rather than data. Decide which reader you are using, then decide what that reader does with that first line.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between csv.reader and csv.DictReader?
choices: reader gives each row as a list; DictReader gives each row as a dict keyed by the header
reader cannot read files with headers
DictReader writes files, reader reads them
questions.explain: DictReader also consumes the header row for you, so row['name'] works and you never count column positions.

questions.prompt: You read a CSV with csv.reader. What type is the age in a row like ['Alice', '25']?
questions.explain: CSV is plain text and carries no types at all. Anything you want to do arithmetic with has to be converted with int() or float() yourself.

questions.prompt: Match each format to what it suits.
right: Simple rows and columns anything can open
questions.explain: The choice is usually decided by the data's shape: flat rows fit CSV, anything nested fits JSON, and Excel is for when a person will open it.

questions.prompt: Reading an .xlsx file in the lesson uses pandas: `df = pd.___('data.xlsx')`.
questions.explain: pandas and openpyxl both have to be installed first. Excel is a binary format, so there is no built-in module for it the way there is for CSV and JSON.

questions.prompt: Which are true of JSON compared with CSV?
choices: It keeps numbers and booleans as numbers and booleans
It is what most APIs reply with
It is easier to open in a spreadsheet
questions.explain: A spreadsheet opens a CSV directly and makes hard work of JSON. That is the one thing CSV still wins on.
